title: The threat of Starlink looms over Quebecor's Telus bid. But are Canadian telecoms actually vulnerable?
summary: In Quebecor’s $31-billion bid to take over Telus, the theme of Canadian sovereignty is emerging front and centre as the Montreal company pitches a merger, in part, to battle the threat of American…

image.caption: The silhouette of Elon Musk and Starlink logo are seen in this illustration taken June 11, 2026. (Dado Ruvic/Reuters)

blocks.text: In Quebecor’s $31-billion bid to take over Telus, the theme of Canadian sovereignty is emerging front and centre as the Montreal company pitches a merger, in part, to battle the threat of American satellite companies like Elon Musk's SpaceX.

But some researchers and critics say those services, particularly the company's Starlink satellite internet subsidiary, are not the threat to traditional Canadian telecoms that Quebecor CEO Pierre Karl Péladeau says it is.

In a Sunday interview with CBC’s Rosemary Barton, Péladeau framed the proposal as a sovereignty measure, noting that Starlink is likely looking to expand its operations. He likened it to Netflix, which he said massively impacted the Canadian broadcasting industry despite not having a licence with the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission.

"If someone thinks that the Starlink business model is to service only some people in Arkansas, they're completely wrong. Their business model is the world, like Netflix's business model was the world," Péladeau said.
"So I think we should inspire our thinking and our mindset according, you know, [to] the mistakes we did regarding broadcasting and we know what is the cost for Canadians to be invaded."
What would a Quebecor-Telus merger mean for your phone bill?
Still, Dwayne Winseck, director of the Global Media and Internet Concentration Project, is cautious of that framing, calling Péladeau’s remarks "rhetorical distractions."

He noted that while Starlink Mobile, SpaceX’s satellite-to-mobile service, aims to expand in the U.S., it isn’t close to competing with the big three carriers in the US — AT&T, T-Mobile and Verizon — which also oppose its cellular ambitions.
And in Canada, SpaceX has stated it does not intend to compete with Canadian telecoms, but rather work with them.
‘Sovereignty challenge is real’
Last week, Quebecor announced it had made a proposal worth $31 billion to take over Telus.

Telus is currently reviewing an enhanced proposal submitted by Quebecor earlier this month, but its leadership has said it has "serious concerns" about whether regulators would ever approve shrinking the telecommunications market.

Based in Montreal, Quebecor is Canada's fourth-largest telecom company. In recent years it has boomed in value since acquiring Freedom Mobile in 2023, and using its competitors' networks to provide mobile service to customers.

Last week, Prime Minister Mark Carney said that under certain circumstances and depending on the market structure, an oligopoly can lead to more competition with fewer players. He did not comment directly on the Quebecor proposal.

items: Quebecor CEO defends Telus bid, cites falling wireless prices and Canada's sovereignty

blocks.text: "Telecom assets are strategic for our country — we all know this. And then therefore, we need to make sure that we're going to be on the same footing," Péladeau told CBC.

With the recent push for more Canadian independence, the idea of supporting domestic businesses has become "so sensible and part of everyday conversation," said David Nieborg, a media professor at the University of Toronto.
He added that there’s a sense that Ottawa has typically been protective of certain industries, like telecoms, shielding Canadian companies from foreign conglomerates.

David Nieborg is a professor of media and platform studies at the University of Toronto. He says a Canadian push for sovereignty makes sense, but in telecommunications, it can be a costly trade-off for consumers. (Submitted by David Nieborg)

Nieborg said he understands the logic of the sovereignty argument. But, he said, "that's the trade-off that has an impact on pricing on Canadian data, and Canadian telecommunication has been notoriously expensive."

"Sovereignty and innovation and competition should not necessarily be at odds with each other," Nieborg said. "The sovereignty challenge is real, but at the very same time it comes at a significant cost, I think, to Canadian consumers."
What is Starlink's reach in Canada?

SpaceX introduced Starlink to Canadians in late 2020, providing an option for low-latency internet service, particularly for remote or rural communities. It later brought Starlink Mobile coverage in 2025, through a partnership with Rogers.

Earlier this year, SpaceX told Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED) that it would offer Starlink Mobile to every interested Canadian carrier, but "Starlink does not plan to offer its own standalone service nor does it plan to deal exclusively with any one carrier."
In July 2025, Rogers trialled Rogers Satellite, a texting and light-data service carried by Starlink satellites. The company took it commercial last December.

Dwayne Winseck is a professor at Carleton University’s School of Journalism and Communication and director of the Global Media and Internet Concentration Project. He says Quebecor's sovereignty argument is 'speculation heaped on speculation.' (Submitted by Dwayne Winseck)
Starlink's potential threat to telecoms is "speculation heaped upon speculation," said Winseck, who tracks communication, internet and media markets in Canada and dozens of other countries.
He noted that the U.S. company is not competing in the same arena as Canadian telecoms providers — rather, it is primarily serving a niche market where the big players are not.

As of 2025, Winseck's research shows Starlink is Canada's fifth largest internet service provider by revenue and sixth largest by subscribers; it only holds about five per cent of internet access revenue in Canada.

"Incumbents ... have failed to serve rural, remote, far north and Indigenous communities for decades and up to a century," Winseck said. "And what does Elon Musk do? Well, he swoops in and provides a service that people really desperately need."

In 2025, SpaceX announced Starlink had over half a million customers across Canada. The country has become its fifth largest market, according to Ookla Research’s 2025 global satellite broadband performance report.
The case for sovereignty

Still, Canada is looking to break Starlink's grip on Arctic military communications, as Ottawa-based defence technology company Dominion Dynamics recently struck a deal with Canadian satellite giant Telesat to develop a homegrown alternative to Starlink’s military variant, Starshield.
In an interview with the New York Times last week, Carney pointed to disruptions in Starshield’s connectivity in Ukraine as motivation.

"You can't unsee that once you've seen it, particularly given the integration of space technology and defence technology," he said. "The issue for us, the issue for the Koreans, the issue for the Japanese, the issue for the Europeans is can we build, at a minimum, a redundant system or a sovereign system?"

Rob McMahon, associate media and technology studies professor at the University of Alberta, said that Starlink is so concentrated in certain parts of the country that it doesn't pose much of a threat to Canadian telecoms outside those particular regions.

"Sometimes this discourse of sovereignty could be leveraged as a way to support the increasing … concentration of ownership and mergers and so on, whereas I don't really see Starlink in that way," he said.

In an emailed statement to CBC News, Péladeau said, "What matters for Canada is not what any one foreign company intends to do today, but whether the country retains control over critical communications infrastructure in the long term."
